classification.reasoning: Purpose: The crate has almost no content (5 meaningful lines total, 4 in build.rs) and an extremely high major version (99.1.0), which aligns with placeholder or dependency-confusion testing patterns as described in [pattern-high-major-version-placeholders]. Sources/Sinks/Flows: The build script attempts to make a TCP network connection (`TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8888")`). While pointing to localhost rather than an external C2 server, a completely empty/stub crate executing arbitrary network connections in a build script (`build.rs`) without any apparent legitimate library function is highly anomalous. Anomalies: Version 99.1.0, zero dependencies, almost no source code, and a build script executing a network call. Conclusion: Although the network call connects to localhost (which lowers the immediate risk of data exfiltration compared to an external IP), the combination of a high major version placeholder pattern and an arbitrary network connection in a stub crate makes it suspicious and indicative of a test or malicious deployment artifact.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: placeholder-style very high version numbers (99.x)
retrieved_context.text: Six of the twenty crates.io reports in the OSSF malicious-packages snapshot of 2026-09-24 concern versions numbered 99.x (99.0.1, 99.1.0, 99.1.1, 99.99.5), several under names that resemble vendor-internal packages (for example amzn-*). In each of those six reports the OpenSSF Package Analysis project states that the package communicated with a domain associated with malicious activity and executed commands associated with malicious behavior. A very high major version on a newly published crate is therefore a cheap metadata signal that is worth combining with other evidence. It is NOT proof of malice on its own: some legitimate crates (for example the rustc-ap-* family) also use very high major versions, so weigh it against crate age, downloads, content and behaviour.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: TrapDoor campaign (May 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A cross-ecosystem attack campaign using build.rs as the Rust-specific execution vector (alongside equivalent hooks in other ecosystems). Demonstrated that the build.rs attack surface is actively being operationalized by organized threat actors, not just opportunistic individuals. Attack category: build.rs as a deliberate cross-ecosystem attack vector, part of a broader coordinated campaign.
